title: File System Fundamentals
summary: What a file system actually gives you on top of raw disk blocks — naming, persistence, attributes, and the operations every program relies on without thinking about it.

slides.markdown:
A disk is just a flat array of numbered blocks — no names, no folders, no idea what a "file" is. The **file system** is the layer that turns that array into names, directories, and byte streams you can `open()`, `read()`, and `write()` without knowing which physical sectors hold your data.

Think of raw disk blocks like a parking lot with only numbered spaces — the file system is the valet service that remembers "Akshay's car is in spaces 14, 15, and 22" and hands it back to you by name. Everything else in this group — inodes, journaling, allocation — is detail on top of this one idea.

slides.sectionTitle: What a file system actually provides
slides.markdown:
Strip away the syntax and a file system provides exactly three things a raw block device does not: **naming** (a human-readable path instead of a block number), **persistence** (data survives a reboot and a power cycle, unlike RAM), and **organization** (directories, metadata, and access rules so thousands of files stay manageable).

A raw disk has none of this — it will happily let you read block 4,000,000 but has no concept of "which file is that." The file system is the bookkeeping layer: a set of on-disk data structures (superblock, inode table, directory entries, free-space maps) plus the kernel code that maintains them consistently as you create, grow, and delete files.

slides.sectionTitle: File attributes: what's tracked beyond the bytes
slides.markdown:
Every file carries metadata that never appears in its content: **name** (in the directory entry, not the file itself), **size** in bytes, **type** (regular, directory, symlink, device), **permissions** (owner/group/other read-write-execute bits), and **timestamps** — `atime` (last access), `mtime` (last content modification), `ctime` (last metadata change, e.g. a `chmod`).

Run `stat myfile.txt` and you're reading this metadata directly — not the file's contents at all. Interview trap: `mtime` and `ctime` are easy to mix up. Editing content bumps both; running `chmod` alone bumps only `ctime`.

```bash
$ stat myfile.txt
  Size: 4096       Blocks: 8
Access: 2026-07-28 09:12:01
Modify: 2026-07-28 09:10:44
Change: 2026-07-28 09:10:44
```

slides.sectionTitle: The file operations underneath every I/O call
slides.markdown:
Every language's file API — Python's `open()`, Java's `FileInputStream`, C's `fopen` — eventually calls the same small set of OS primitives: **create**, **open** (get a handle, checking permissions), **read**, **write**, **seek** (move the current position without reading), **close** (release the handle), and **delete** (unlink the name).

`open()` doesn't touch disk data — it looks up the path, checks permissions, and hands back a **file descriptor**, a small integer the process uses for every subsequent call. That indirection is why closing a descriptor is cheap and why two processes can hold independent positions into the same file.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the file system as a layer over raw disk blocks
slides.markdown:
![application to disk block layer stack](assets/fs-layer-stack.svg)

Applications never see block numbers. Every path you open gets translated — directory entry to inode to a specific set of blocks — by the file system layer sitting between your code and the disk.

This indirection is what makes `mv` on the same disk instant (only the directory entry changes) while copying to a different disk is slow (every block must actually move).

slides.sectionTitle: File types: regular, directory, and special files
slides.markdown:
Unix treats almost everything as "a file," but three types matter for this group: **regular files** (your actual data — text, binaries, images), **directories** (a special file whose content is a table of name-to-inode mappings, covered in the next group's topic), and **special/device files** (`/dev/sda`, `/dev/null`) that don't hold data at all — they're handles the kernel routes to a device driver.

`ls -l` shows the type in the first column: `-` for regular, `d` for directory, `b`/`c` for block/character device, `l` for symlink. This unification is deliberate: it's why `cat /dev/urandom` "works" the same way `cat file.txt` does, even though one reads a disk and the other reads a hardware entropy source.

Every read or write happens at some **position** in the file, and how you move that position has real performance consequences.

| | Sequential access | Direct (random) access |
|---|---|---|
| Position moves | Automatically forward after each read/write | Jumps anywhere via `seek()` (`lseek` in C) |
| Good for | Log files, streaming media, tape (historically) | Databases, indexed lookups, memory-mapped files |
| HDD cost | Cheap — one seek, then the arm just tracks | Expensive — a seek (~5-10ms) per jump |
| SSD cost | Fast | Also fast — no mechanical seek penalty |

**How to decide:** if your access pattern is "read the whole thing in order," design for sequential I/O even on SSDs — larger reads still amortize per-I/O overhead better than many small random ones.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming delete instantly frees disk space
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I ran `rm bigfile.log` and `df` should immediately show the space back."

**Why it's wrong:** `unlink()` (what `rm` calls) only removes the directory entry pointing to the inode. If another process still has the file open — a classic pattern for log rotation — the inode and its blocks stay allocated until the last open file descriptor closes. You can `rm` a 50GB log a running process is still writing to and see zero space freed until that process exits or closes the handle.

**Correct model:** deletion is reference-counted. Space is only reclaimed when a file's **link count** (names pointing to it) and **open descriptor count** both hit zero. `lsof +L1` finds these "deleted but still open" files on a disk that mysteriously won't free up.

slides.sectionTitle: The file descriptor table and why fork() shares positions
slides.markdown:
A process's open files live in a **file descriptor table**, each entry pointing to a kernel-wide **open file table** entry that tracks the current position and access mode. Two independent `open()` calls on the same path get separate positions; but a `fork()`'d child shares its parent's open file table entries, so a `seek()` in one is visible in the other.

This is why shell redirection (`cmd > file`) works the way it does: the shell opens the file once, then `fork`+`exec`s the command, which inherits that exact descriptor — parent and child would see the same write position if both wrote to it.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: what open() costs vs what read() costs
slides.markdown:
`open()` on a warm directory cache typically costs low single-digit microseconds — a few hash lookups and a permission check. A cold `open()` that has to fault in inode data from disk can cost 1-10ms on an HDD, far more than the read that follows. `read()` of already-cached data (in the page cache) costs roughly the same as a `memcpy` — sub-microsecond per 4KB page; a genuine disk read behind it costs 0.1-10ms depending on HDD vs SSD.

The practical lesson: opening a file repeatedly in a hot loop (a common anti-pattern) is often more expensive than the actual I/O you're trying to do — cache the descriptor instead of re-opening.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: what different layers mean by "file"
slides.markdown:
"File" means something different depending on which layer of the stack you ask.

| Layer | What "file" means |
|---|---|
| Application | A named, typed object with content — `report.pdf` |
| Kernel VFS | An inode plus a set of operations (`read`, `write`, `mmap`) — filesystem-agnostic |
| File system driver (ext4, NTFS) | An inode number plus block pointers on this specific disk layout |
| Disk controller | Nothing — just logical block addresses it's told to read or write |

**How to decide:** when debugging "my file operation is slow," figure out which layer is actually the bottleneck — a slow `open()` is usually VFS/directory-cache, a slow `read()` is usually the disk or its underlying block layout.
